paragraphs: Prediction competitions recruit many people to improve a model, but their reward structures can create weaknesses in participants’ incentives. This paper proposes a Crowdsourced Learning Mechanism that makes collaboration part of the competition itself. Participants work on a shared prediction hypothesis, giving them a common object to improve as the process continues.

The mechanism borrows from prediction markets, where participants put money behind judgments about future events. Here, the mechanism continually publishes its current hypothesis, and a participant can wager on a proposed modification. The contribution being evaluated is therefore an update to the shared predictor, with a financial stake attached to that update.

The central incentive property connects a participant’s profit to how much the update improves performance on a released test set. This makes the reward sensitive to the contribution’s measured value. The paper’s contribution is a mechanism for organizing collaborative prediction work: it connects public, incremental model development with payments that scale according to the improvement each participant supplies.
neurips-2011-a-collaborative-mechanism-f.tldr: A prediction-market-inspired mechanism rewards participants according to how much their updates improve a shared predictor on a released test set.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs entries missing from a partially observed table of values. Many methods assume the entire matrix has low rank, meaning its entries follow a relatively compact global structure. This paper introduces a broader perspective based on denoising: a missing value should be predictable from nearby points, allowing local relationships to guide reconstruction.

The proposed nonparametric procedure repeatedly averages information within local neighborhoods using mean-shift. It can also be constrained to preserve a locally low-rank manifold structure. That option combines neighborhood-based smoothing with a local geometric constraint. The denoising scale, neighborhood size, local dimensionality, and iteration count can be chosen by cross-validating reconstruction error.

The authors apply these algorithms after an initial reconstruction, which can come from a low-rank method. They report consistent improvements on synthetic data, images, and motion-capture data. These findings support denoising as a useful refinement stage: an initial estimate supplies completed values, and local structure provides additional information for improving them in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2011-a-denoising-view-of-matrix-.tldr: Local denoising improves initial matrix completions by using neighborhood relationships, with consistent gains on the reported datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to detect a difference between the means of two multivariate normal distributions when there are many measured variables. The setting allows the number of variables to exceed the sample size. Its proposed test combines a random projection of the observations with the classical Hotelling T-squared statistic.

The theoretical analysis considers a regime in which both dimension and sample size grow. Within that framework, the authors derive the test’s asymptotic power, describing its ability to detect a mean shift. They then establish sufficient conditions under which it has greater power than other leading tests. The advantage is therefore tied to specified conditions, rather than asserted for every high-dimensional problem.

Simulated comparisons using ROC curves show stronger performance in the parameter regimes predicted by the theory. A further comparison on gene-expression data illustrates an advantage when distinguishing cancer types. Together, these results connect the mathematical conditions to observed behavior and support random projection as a useful component of high-dimensional mean testing.
neurips-2011-a-more-powerful-two-sample-.tldr: Combining random projection with Hotelling’s statistic yields a high-dimensional mean test with greater power under sufficient conditions supported by experiments.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation asks how valuable it is to follow a given policy from different states. This paper addresses systems with continuous states, where evaluation must account for a space of possible states rather than just a finite list. It proposes a nonparametric representation of the system built using kernel density estimation.

For this estimated model, the authors determine the form of the value function and compute it using Galerkin’s method. The distinction between the modeled system and the original system matters: the stated characterization concerns the value function associated with the kernel-based model. This provides a concrete route from a statistical system representation to policy evaluation.

The paper also uses Galerkin’s method to connect several existing approaches. Least-Squares Temporal Difference learning, Kernelized Temporal Difference learning, discrete-state dynamic programming, and the proposed method can all be derived through this common framework. In the reported numerical evaluation, the new approach performs better than the others. Its contribution combines an evaluation algorithm with a unified view of related methods.
neurips-2011-a-non-parametric-approach-t.tldr: A kernel-based system model enables continuous-state policy evaluation and connects several established evaluation methods through Galerkin’s method.

paragraphs: An additive function expresses an output as a sum of component functions, each using only a subset of the input variables. This paper builds a Gaussian process model around that structure. Such a representation makes it possible to describe a complex relationship through smaller pieces, including interactions among selected groups of variables.

The model generalizes both Generalized Additive Models and standard Gaussian processes with squared-exponential kernels. Its key computational contribution is a kernel parameterization that supports efficient evaluation of all input interaction terms, even though their number grows exponentially with input dimension. The authors also interpret hyperparameter learning as a Bayesian form of Hierarchical Kernel Learning.

The resulting structure offers more than a way to calculate predictions: it can make the relationships captured by the model easier to interpret. The paper reports state-of-the-art predictive performance on regression tasks alongside this increased interpretability. Its stated contribution is therefore a tractable way to combine a rich range of interactions with an additive description of the learned function.
neurips-2011-additive-gaussian-processes.tldr: Additive Gaussian processes efficiently model many input interactions while offering interpretable structure and strong reported regression performance.

paragraphs: Selective classification allows a predictor to abstain on some inputs. This paper asks whether that option can let a learner track the classification performance of the best unknown hypothesis in its class. It establishes that this is theoretically possible when the associated excess-loss class satisfies a specified Bernstein condition.

The guarantee also controls how much of the input distribution is rejected. The probability mass of the abstention region decreases at a rate involving the sample size, the Bernstein parameters, and Hanneke’s disagreement coefficient. This links competitive classification performance to increasing prediction coverage under the stated assumption. However, the strategy faces computational barriers because it requires empirical error minimization in an agnostic setting.

To obtain a usable algorithm, the authors heuristically approximate the theoretical strategy with constrained support vector machines. In their experiments, this method consistently outperforms the traditional rejection rule based on distance from the decision boundary. The paper thus supplies both a conditional theoretical guarantee and an empirically successful approximation, with different forms of support for each.
neurips-2011-agnostic-selective-classifi.tldr: Under a Bernstein condition, abstention can track the best classifier with shrinking rejection, motivating an effective constrained-SVM approximation.

paragraphs: A planning system needs an action model to predict what its actions will do. This paper introduces two frameworks for learning such models while using them to construct plans. Both frameworks measure learning progress through planning behavior, making failures and attempts part of the formal account of how learning proceeds.

In mistake-bounded planning, the learner receives a planner for its model representation, a simulator, and a generator of planning problems. Its goal is to learn with at most a polynomial number of faulty plans. In planned exploration, the learner has no problem generator. It must choose its own problems, plan for them, and converge within a polynomial number of planning attempts.

The authors reduce learning in these settings to concept learning with one-sided error and provide successful algorithms for both frameworks. They also identify a particular family of hypothesis spaces that is efficiently learnable in each. This gives a formal basis for autonomous model acquisition while keeping the efficiency claim tied to the demonstrated family of model spaces.
neurips-2011-autonomous-learning-of-acti.tldr: Two frameworks formalize learning action models through planning, with polynomial bounds and efficient learning for a specific family of hypothesis spaces.

paragraphs: When a function is expensive to evaluate, optimization must choose carefully which inputs to test. Standard budgeted formulations often select one experiment at a time and limit only the total number of evaluations. This paper broadens the problem to include scheduling concerns that arise when experiments can overlap and take uncertain amounts of time.

The formulation allows concurrent experiments, treats their durations as stochastic, and constrains both the experiment count and total experimental time. These features make the schedule part of the optimization problem. A useful collection of evaluations must fit the available time as well as the evaluation budget, while accounting for uncertainty about when experiments will finish.

The authors develop offline and online algorithms for selecting concurrent experiments in this setting. Tests on multiple optimization benchmarks show highly effective schedules compared with natural baselines. The stated result supports treating experiment selection and scheduling together: the new formulation captures resource constraints that a purely sequential evaluation budget leaves out, and the proposed algorithms perform well in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2011-budgeted-optimization-with-.tldr: A broader optimization framework schedules parallel experiments with uncertain durations under both evaluation-count and time budgets.

paragraphs: Complex, noisy data can contain a much simpler underlying shape. In some cases that shape resembles a network, such as a road system or a collection of trajectories. This paper develops a framework for extracting a one-dimensional graph skeleton from unorganized data, making such structure available as a compact object for analysis.

The framework uses Reeb graphs to both extract and simplify the skeleton. The proposed algorithm can work with high-dimensional point clouds or proximity graphs, does not require complex optimization, and can represent arbitrary graph structures. That flexibility matters when the desired summary has a graph structure that a single curve cannot adequately express.

The authors give theoretical results supporting the method and demonstrate it through experiments, including comparisons with principal curves. These experiments support its effectiveness and generality in the tested settings. The broader contribution is a simple, practical route from unorganized observations to a graph summary, bringing skeleton extraction and simplification together within one framework.
neurips-2011-data-skeletonization-via-re.tldr: A Reeb-graph framework extracts and simplifies graph-shaped skeletons from unorganized high-dimensional data without complex optimization.

paragraphs: Online learning updates predictions as information arrives. The paper introduces an algorithmic approach outside the mirror-descent and follow-the-leader families that commonly underpin online learning methods. Its construction combines random playout with randomized rounding of loss subgradients, bringing these two randomized ingredients into a single learning procedure.

One application is collaborative filtering with trace-norm-constrained matrices. In this setting, predictions are represented by a matrix whose complexity is restricted through its trace norm. The authors provide what they identify as the first computationally efficient online algorithm for that problem. The significance is computational as well as statistical: the contribution supplies an efficient procedure for carrying out learning under the stated matrix constraint.

A second application resolves an open question connecting batch learning with transductive online learning. This shows that the proposed approach also contributes to understanding relationships between learning settings. Together, the applications establish the method’s value in two ways: it enables an efficient algorithm for a concrete prediction problem and supplies a result about the relationship between learning frameworks.
neurips-2011-efficient-online-learning-v.tldr: Random playout and randomized rounding yield an efficient online collaborative-filtering algorithm and resolve a question linking batch and transductive learning.

paragraphs: Speech recordings mix information about the speaker with information about words, language, and recording conditions. A representation that preserves all of these can introduce irrelevant variation into speaker recognition. This paper proposes a deep Siamese architecture that extracts speaker-specific information from MFCC acoustic features, aiming to make the representation better suited to identifying speakers.

The training objective combines several goals. It learns characteristics associated with speaker identity while regularizing the representation to normalize interference from non-speaker information and avoid information loss. This addresses the tension between suppressing distracting variation and preserving useful information. The method therefore changes the acoustic representation itself as part of the recognition approach.

Experiments on LDC benchmark corpora and a Chinese speech corpus show that the learned representation is insensitive to spoken text, language, and environmental mismatches in the reported evaluations. It also outperforms MFCCs and other leading speaker-recognition techniques in those comparisons. These findings support learning task-specific speech features as a way to reduce interference from other information carried by speech.
neurips-2011-extracting-speaker-specific.tldr: A regularized Siamese network learns speaker-specific acoustic features that improve recognition across the reported text, language, and environmental variations.

paragraphs: This paper considers k-means clustering when the dataset cannot fit in main memory and must be read sequentially, for example from disk. The goal is to cluster effectively while using very little memory. That setting makes the practical costs of an algorithm central, because a theoretically attractive method may still require too much storage or computation.

Building on recent theoretical work, the authors simplify an existing algorithm in both its design and analysis. Their changes remove large constant factors from the approximation guarantee, memory requirements, and running time. These improvements address several practical obstacles together, connecting the quality of the resulting clustering with the resources needed to produce it.

The method additionally incorporates approximate nearest-neighbor search to obtain computation below the n-times-k scale, where n is the number of points and k is the number of clusters. The authors report favorable theoretical and experimental comparisons with existing methods. The contribution is an approach designed to retain strong clustering performance under sequential-access and memory constraints.
neurips-2011-fast-and-accurate-k-means-f.tldr: A simplified, memory-efficient k-means algorithm combines theoretical improvements with approximate nearest-neighbor search for large sequentially accessed datasets.

paragraphs: Learning algorithms often optimize a surrogate loss because the task’s actual loss is difficult to work with directly. This paper studies latent structural versions of probit and ramp losses. Its central question is whether optimizing these substitutes can lead to predictors whose task performance approaches the best achievable within the chosen linear prediction class.

The authors prove a strong consistency result for both losses. For any feature map, including infinite-dimensional ones, the resulting predictors approach the infimum task loss available to linear predictors over those features. The reference point is therefore the best performance permitted by that feature representation and predictor class. The result establishes that both surrogate choices can target that reference point.

The paper also supplies finite-sample generalization bounds describing convergence rates. These bounds suggest faster convergence for probit loss, while ramp loss is easier to optimize and may be more practical. This distinction matters when selecting a training objective: a stronger suggested statistical rate and an easier optimization problem favor different losses.
neurips-2011-generalization-bounds-and-c.tldr: Both latent structural losses are consistent within the chosen linear class, with bounds favoring probit statistically and optimization favoring ramp practically.

paragraphs: Many text collections attach multiple labels to a document, and those labels often belong to a hierarchy. Product categories and diagnosis codes are examples: their organization contains information beyond the individual labels. This paper introduces hierarchically supervised latent Dirichlet allocation, or HSLDA, for bag-of-word data with both hierarchical and multiple labels.

The primary goal is to predict labels for previously unseen documents. A second interest is obtaining improved lower-dimensional representations of the text. The model brings the structure of the labels into this learning problem, allowing the organization of categories to inform the relationship between a document’s words and its assigned labels.

The authors demonstrate HSLDA on large-scale clinical document labeling and retail product categorization tasks. In those evaluations, using the hierarchical label structure substantially improves prediction on unseen examples compared with models that do not use it. The findings support treating a label hierarchy as useful supervision, with value for prediction beyond simply knowing which labels appear on each training document.
neurips-2011-hierarchically-supervised-l.tldr: HSLDA uses hierarchical, multiple labels to improve prediction for unseen text documents in clinical and retail evaluations.

paragraphs: Predicting the effectiveness of HIV combination therapies is complicated by how clinical datasets represent patients and treatments. Patients have different treatment backgrounds, levels of therapy experience are unevenly represented, and some treatment-history information is missing. Therapies and their outcomes are also represented unevenly. The proposed approach addresses these issues together.

This joint treatment matters because the prediction problem includes variation in both patient history and the available evidence about therapies. The paper’s history distribution matching approach is designed around that data situation. Its stated comparison is with a commonly used approach that does not account for these issues, making the handling of clinical-data differences central to the evaluation.

Computational validation on clinical data shows significantly higher predictive power for the proposed model. The advantage is especially pronounced for patients with longer treatment histories and for samples involving rare therapies. For the remaining samples, the model is at least as powerful in the reported evaluation. These are findings about predicting therapy effectiveness from the evaluated clinical data.
neurips-2011-history-distribution-matchi.tldr: Accounting jointly for treatment-history differences, missing information, and data imbalance improves reported predictions of HIV combination-therapy effectiveness.

paragraphs: Bayes’ rule updates prior information using evidence to produce a posterior distribution. This paper develops a nonparametric version of that update using kernel representations of probabilities in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The approach provides a way to carry out Bayesian inference through sample-based representations of distributions.

The prior is represented by an empirical kernel mean, while conditional probabilities are represented through empirical covariance operators. The method then computes the posterior’s kernel mean as a weighted sample. In this representation, the update produces sample weights that describe the posterior through its kernel mean, connecting the mathematical probability update to a sample-based computational result.

The authors demonstrate the method in Bayesian computation without a likelihood and in filtering with a nonparametric state-space model. They also establish a consistency rate for the posterior estimate, giving theoretical support for its convergence. These contributions combine a general construction of a kernel-based Bayesian update with applications and a quantitative convergence result for the resulting posterior representation.
neurips-2011-kernel-bayes-rule-214902893.tldr: Kernel Bayes’ rule computes a sample-based posterior representation for nonparametric Bayesian inference, with applications and a consistency rate.

paragraphs: Sparse representations describe an observation using relatively few elements from a dictionary adapted to the data. Learning these representations becomes computationally demanding when both the observations and the dictionary are large. This paper addresses that cost through screening, random projections, and a hierarchical learning framework that combines the two.

The screening tests quickly identify dictionary codewords guaranteed to receive zero weights. This provides a principled way to recognize elements that will not contribute to a representation. The authors also study random projections specifically in the context of sparse representation learning, examining their role in a setting where reducing computational effort is a central concern.

The final framework uses incremental random projections and screening to learn a hierarchically structured dictionary in small stages. Its staged construction brings the two computational ideas into one learning process. Empirical results show that it learns informative hierarchical sparse representations more efficiently. The paper therefore contributes both guaranteed screening tests and an empirically supported framework for making large sparse-representation problems more manageable.
neurips-2011-learning-sparse-representat.tldr: Guaranteed screening and incremental random projections make hierarchical sparse-representation learning more efficient in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer a reward function from observed behavior. A central difficulty is ambiguity: typically, infinitely many reward functions can make the same behavior optimal. This paper addresses the selection problem through a Bayesian framework, using maximum a posteriori estimation to choose a reward function.

Maximum a posteriori estimation selects a reward function with the highest posterior support under the model. This gives a criterion for choosing among reward functions compatible with the behavior data. The authors also show that most previous inverse reinforcement learning algorithms can be represented within their framework, connecting existing approaches through a common formulation of reward estimation.

To compute the estimate, the paper presents a gradient method based on differentiability or subdifferentiability of the posterior distribution. Comparisons with earlier algorithms demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The contribution brings together a Bayesian selection criterion, a unifying view of previous methods, and an optimization procedure for finding a reward estimate despite the ambiguity inherent in observed behavior.
neurips-2011-map-inference-for-bayesian-.tldr: A Bayesian MAP framework selects among ambiguous reward functions and supports a gradient-based inverse reinforcement learning method.

paragraphs: In a discrete probabilistic graphical model, an inference task may require choosing values for some variables while averaging over uncertainty in others. This paper studies that combination: it seeks maximum a posteriori estimates for designated variables and marginalizes the remaining variables. The two groups are described as max nodes and sum nodes.

The proposed algorithm passes a mixture of max and sum messages through the model, choosing the message type according to the source node. The authors derive this hybrid procedure from a relaxation of a variational framework. That derivation gives the algorithm an optimization-based foundation and explains how the two forms of inference fit into one procedure.

The paper further shows that Expectation Maximization can be viewed as an approximation to the proposed algorithm. This connects the new method to a familiar approach for inference involving latent variables. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, with several baselines, demonstrate its effectiveness. The result is an approximate inference method built explicitly around the different roles of selected and marginalized variables.
neurips-2011-message-passing-for-approxi.tldr: A variationally derived hybrid message-passing algorithm combines maximization over selected variables with marginalization over latent variables.

paragraphs: This paper studies minimizing a convex objective when only unbiased estimates of its gradients are available. The objective is defined on a Hilbert space, a setting that includes kernel logistic regression and least-squares regression. The authors analyze stochastic gradient descent and a modification that averages the successive iterates.

Their analysis is non-asymptotic, describing convergence after a finite number of iterations. It suggests that a learning rate decreasing inversely with the iteration count can achieve the optimal convergence rate under strong convexity. However, that choice is sensitive to both the absence of strong convexity and the constant that scales the learning rate.

The proposed remedy is to combine a more slowly decreasing learning rate with averaging. The analysis finds that this combination robustly reaches the optimal convergence rate in the setting studied. Simulations on synthetic and standard datasets illustrate the theoretical results. The practical message is that learning-rate decay and averaging should be considered together, because their combination affects both convergence and sensitivity to tuning.
neurips-2011-non-asymptotic-analysis-of-.tldr: Finite-iteration analysis supports slower learning-rate decay with iterate averaging as a robust route to optimal stochastic-optimization convergence.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes support vector machines used for regularized least-squares regression with Gaussian radial-basis-function kernels. The central question is how quickly prediction quality improves as more data becomes available. The authors establish a new oracle inequality, giving a theoretical tool for assessing the performance of this regression procedure.

The proof uses the modulus of smoothness, which expresses the smoothness properties relevant to the analysis. From the oracle inequality, the authors derive learning rates. They also show that a simple parameter-selection method based on the data can achieve those rates. This connects the theoretical performance result to a way of choosing the method’s parameters from observed data.

The resulting rates are asymptotically optimal for regression functions satisfying certain standard smoothness conditions. Both parts of that qualification matter: optimality describes the large-sample behavior and applies to the specified smoothness setting. The contribution is a linked set of guarantees, moving from an oracle inequality to achievable rates and then to conditional asymptotic optimality.
neurips-2011-optimal-learning-rates-for-.tldr: Gaussian-kernel least-squares SVMs achieve asymptotically optimal rates under stated smoothness conditions, including with simple data-dependent parameter selection.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing aims to recover sparse vectors from a small set of fixed linear measurements. This paper introduces a partial hard-thresholding operator that generates a family of iterative recovery algorithms. The family connects established hard-thresholding methods with a new procedure called Orthogonal Matching Pursuit with Replacement, or OMPR.

Like ordinary Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, OMPR adds one coordinate based on its correlation with the current residual. It also removes one coordinate, allowing the active set to change through replacement. This modification supports strong recovery guarantees under the Restricted Isometry Property, a condition on the measurement matrix. The authors describe their guarantees as the best known in that framework.

An extension called OMPR-Hash uses locality-sensitive hashing and is presented as the first sparse-recovery algorithm with provably sublinear complexity in dimensionality. The proof techniques also sharpen analyses of CoSaMP and Subspace Pursuit. Experiments recover vectors with up to a million dimensions and show greater speed and robustness than existing methods on the large problems evaluated.
neurips-2011-orthogonal-matching-pursuit.tldr: Allowing coordinate replacement strengthens greedy sparse recovery, while a hashing extension provides provably sublinear computation in dimensionality.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning considers several prediction tasks together so their relationships can inform learning. This paper proposes a sparse Bayesian model for both regression and classification. It captures correlations between tasks through a low-rank approximation of their covariance matrix while also encouraging sparsity in the features used for prediction.

The authors introduce a family of priors that encourage group sparsity, built from matrix-variate Gaussian scale mixtures. These priors provide the model’s mechanism for favoring sparse feature structure. The amount of sparsity can be learned from data by combining approximate inference with type II maximum likelihood estimation of the hyperparameters, making sparsity itself part of the estimation process.

Evaluations on biology and vision datasets demonstrate the model’s applicability to regression and classification. Its predictive performance is competitive with previously proposed methods in those experiments. The contribution combines two forms of structure in one Bayesian model: a compact account of task correlations and sparse feature use, with a data-driven procedure for setting the strength of sparsity.
neurips-2011-sparse-bayesian-multi-task-.tldr: A Bayesian multi-task model jointly learns sparse feature use and low-rank task correlations, achieving competitive reported predictive performance.

paragraphs: Image segmentation groups an image into regions, making spatial relationships relevant to the grouping process. This paper studies the distance-dependent Chinese restaurant process in that setting. The model favors grouping data points that are close according to an external distance, allowing location to influence how a partition is formed.

The authors examine the biases introduced by the spatial model and propose a hierarchical extension better suited to producing segmentations resembling human judgments. They also study sensitivity to hyperparameters governing distance and appearance. This makes the work an investigation of both the model’s structural preferences and how its behavior changes with those choices.

The paper presents what it describes as the first rigorous comparison of nonparametric Bayesian models for image segmentation. In unsupervised segmentation, the results show that substantially simpler models and algorithms can achieve performance similar to existing alternatives. The finding supports simplicity as a practical advantage in this setting while preserving the empirical claim of comparable, rather than universally superior, segmentation performance.
neurips-2011-spatial-distance-dependent-.tldr: Spatial and hierarchical distance-dependent clustering models achieve comparable unsupervised segmentation performance with substantially simpler models and algorithms.

paragraphs: Boosting builds a predictor by repeatedly training weak learners. This paper proposes VadaBoost, an algorithm motivated by empirical Bernstein bounds that balances the sample mean and sample variance of exponential loss. Its objective therefore considers both the average loss and how much that loss varies across the training sample.

The main computational contribution is how each boosting step is performed. VadaBoost supplies weighted data to a weak learner to minimize its cost efficiently. Earlier empirical Bernstein boosting methods required evaluating every possible weak learner by brute force. Removing that enumeration requirement lets the variance-sensitive objective work with a much broader choice of weak learner.

Experiments show that VadaBoost retains the performance improvements associated with EBBoost while extending beyond decision stumps to handle arbitrary weak learners. The reported comparisons include significant gains over AdaBoost with weak learners such as CART decision trees. The contribution is therefore both an objective that penalizes loss variability and an efficient training procedure that makes that objective usable with richer learners.
neurips-2011-variance-penalizing-adaboos.tldr: VadaBoost efficiently balances mean and variance of exponential loss, extending empirical-Bernstein boosting to arbitrary weak learners with reported performance gains.
